source: Normann & Morina (2018) The efficacy of metacognitive therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Updated meta-analysis of MCT (Wells) for psychological complaints. Large pre-post effects and large win over waitlist.
numbers: 25 studies (15 RCTs), 780 adults. Pre-post g=1.72, follow-up g=1.57. Versus waitlist g=2.06 (9 trials). Only one child/adolescent trial.
limits: Few trials per comparison; risk of bias unclear or high in almost a third of studies; uncontrolled pre-post effects are inflated.
agent_relevance: Clinical MCT targets beliefs about thinking and worry loops. The effect sizes show the human intervention works but say nothing about LLMs.

source: Normann & Morina (2018) The efficacy of metacognitive therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis (MCT vs CBT)
finding: MCT beat other therapies, mostly CBT, but the edge shrank at follow-up. Authors warn it needs caution.
numbers: MCT vs CBT g=0.69 post-treatment (k=8) and g=0.37 at follow-up (k=7). Earlier meta-analysis (Normann 2014, 5 trials) had g=0.97.
limits: Lower confidence bound near zero at follow-up; heterogeneity across studies; effect fell as more trials arrived (0.97 to 0.69).
agent_relevance: Shrinking effects with more trials: discount early large effects when judging any metacognitive scaffold.

source: Normann & Morina (2018) The efficacy of metacognitive therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis (allegiance check)
finding: 13 of the trials were co-authored by the founder, Wells. Their effects were larger, but not significantly so once one outlier was removed.
numbers: Wells-group g=1.98 (95% CI 1.52-2.44) vs independent g=1.49 (1.17-1.81); p=0.09. Without the Dammen 2015 outlier: g=1.84, k=12, p=0.19.
quote: Because 13 of the trials were co-authored by the originator of MCT (Adrian Wells), the possibility of allegiance bias was examined
limits: Only one trial (Nordahl 2018) had balanced CBT and MCT originators on the author list; allegiance cannot be ruled out.
agent_relevance: Founder-run evaluations overstate gains. A self-built agent scaffold needs independent evaluation too.

source: Hagen et al. (2017) Metacognitive therapy for depression in adults: a waiting list randomized controlled trial with six months follow-up
finding: Early MCT depression RCT: 10 sessions beat a 10-week waitlist with very large effects.
numbers: N=39 randomised. Controlled effect sizes d=2.51 (depression) and d=1.92 (anxiety). About 70-80% recovered after MCT and at 6 months; 5% of waitlist recovered. 2 dropouts in waitlist, 0 in MCT.
limits: Tiny sample, waitlist control (no active comparator), same group as the founder.
agent_relevance: Waitlist designs inflate effects. Treat gains measured against waitlist controls as upper bounds.

source: Gjengedal et al. (2025) Metacognitive therapy and work-focus for patients with depression, anxiety or comorbid on sick leave: open-label RCT (eClinicalMedicine)
finding: Large pragmatic RCT. Immediate MCT plus work focus raised return to work and cut symptoms versus waiting; the waitlist group caught up after its own treatment.
numbers: N=236 (121 immediate, 115 waitlist). Registry return-to-work at 12 weeks 39% (47/121) vs 20% (23/115), OR 2.39 (1.32-4.32). Self-report 42% vs 18%, OR 3.44. Time x group coefficients: anxiety -8.35, depression -10.84.
limits: Open-label, waitlist control, single centre in Norway; Wells among authors; welfare-system effects.
agent_relevance: Shows an organisational outcome (work) can move with a thinking-about-thinking intervention. Catch-up means the gain is speed, not a different end state.

source: Anwar et al. (2026) Impact of metacognitive therapy on OCD severity and beliefs: three-wave multisite RCT with panel mediation (Depression and Anxiety)
finding: Independent non-Western trial supports MCT for OCD, but the central theory step (belief change comes first) failed.
numbers: N=76 (38 MCT, 38 TAU), 12 weekly sessions, assessor-blinded. Y-BOCS mean difference -4.00 post and -6.92 at 6 months (both p<0.001). Prespecified lagged indirect effect through beliefs beta=-0.01, not supported.
quote: broad metacognitive belief domains behave as markers of clinical state rather than proximal mechanisms
limits: Comparison is treatment as usual, not an active therapy; small N; exploratory mediation model.
agent_relevance: Outcome gains can hold while the proposed mechanism fails. Do not assume a scaffold works for the reason its theory says.

source: Penney et al. (2022) Immediate and sustained outcomes and moderators associated with metacognitive training for psychosis (JAMA Psychiatry)
finding: MCT for psychosis (Moritz group training aimed at cognitive biases and overconfidence) gives small to moderate gains that last up to a year.
numbers: 43 studies, N=1816 in meta-analysis. Positive symptoms g=0.50, delusions 0.69, hallucinations 0.26, cognitive biases 0.16 (0.03-0.29), negative symptoms 0.23, functioning 0.41, self-esteem 0.17. Quality of life 0.20 (ns).
limits: Publication bias present for hallucinations, cognitive biases, negative symptoms, self-esteem, QoL. Lower-quality studies gave smaller distal effects (Q=9.33, p=.05). High heterogeneity post-test. Only moderator: publication year for hallucinations (beta=0.04).
agent_relevance: The direct target (cognitive biases) has the smallest effect (0.16). Belief-doubt training works through symptoms, not bias scores.

source: Metacognitive training for schizophrenia: a systematic review (Shanghai Archives of Psychiatry, 2015)
finding: Earlier review found evidence too weak to conclude MCT works for schizophrenia.
numbers: 10 RCTs from 54 reports. Pooled 4 studies PANSS positive: small significant gain for MCT. Pooled 4 studies PSYRATS delusions: no significant difference. Other outcomes mixed.
limits: Different outcome measures; few ITT analyses; methodological problems. Later meta-analysis (Penney 2022) disagrees (delusions g=0.69).
agent_relevance: Conflicting meta-analyses on the same intervention show conclusions flip with more and better trials.

source: Goncalves et al. (2026) Baseline cognitive insight moderates the efficacy of metacognitive training for psychosis: individual participant data (Front Psychol)
finding: Individual-participant analysis: people with low baseline insight gain most from MCT; ceiling effects hid gains in earlier trials.
numbers: 614 participants, 13 studies (PERMEPSY). Significant Group x Baseline interactions on all Beck Cognitive Insight Scale scores. 26.5% already scored high-insight at baseline.
limits: Secondary analysis; self-report scale; does not show symptom change; cross-study harmonisation.
agent_relevance: Baseline metacognitive state moderates benefit. A scaffold that adds self-checks probably helps weaker reasoners more than strong ones.

source: Bahrami, Olsen, Bang, Roepstorff, Rees, Frith (2012) What failure in collective decision-making tells us about metacognition (Phil Trans R Soc B)
finding: Dyads share confidence like cues in multisensory integration. Two heads beat one only when members are similarly sensitive; if one is much worse, the pair does worse than the better member.
numbers: Experiment 2 (2x2 design): verbal talk alone was near optimal for similar sensitivities; adding a non-verbal confidence tool significantly reduced performance (collective benefit crowded out). With noise added to one partner, dyad sensitivity was significantly worse than the better observer in the verbal condition.
quote: These failures provide an exquisite opportunity to understand human communication of metacognitive confidence
limits: Perceptual two-alternative task, lab dyads; the weighted-confidence-sharing model is a benchmark, not a universal rule. Exact test statistics not extracted.
agent_relevance: Design rule for multi-agent LLMs: pooling helps only if agents are about equally reliable; confidence weighting needs calibration.

source: Pescetelli, Rees, Bahrami (2016) The perceptual and social components of metacognition (JEP General)
finding: Confidence (wager) is built from sensory evidence plus social agreement; agreement and disagreement shift wagers in opposite, unequal directions and add linearly.
numbers: Dyads did a visual decision task alone then together. Sensory and social contributions to wagers were linearly additive. Dyad members' average metacognitive sensitivity correlated positively with dyadic performance and benefit over average individual performance.
limits: Perceptual task; wagers only; dyads of strangers. Correlation sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Peer agreement is a legitimate confidence input but should be weighted separately from own evidence.

source: Vuillaume, Martin, Sackur, Cleeremans (2020) Comparing self- and hetero-metacognition in the absence of verbal communication (PLoS ONE)
finding: People can read another person's confidence as accurately as they judge their own; cues differ by context. Supports a shared inference route for metacognition and theory of mind.
numbers: Auditory task; participants judged own or others' confidence, live or on a recorded video of themselves. Accuracy of others' confidence reading matched self-evaluation (abstract-level; per-condition statistics not extracted).
limits: Statistics not extracted; lab task, small cue set.
agent_relevance: Supports one calibration module reused for modelling both own and peer uncertainty.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Large battery vs 1,907 humans. GPT-4 matched or beat humans on false belief, indirect requests and misdirection, but struggled on faux pas. LLaMA2's faux pas win was a bias toward saying 'ignorance'.
numbers: GPT-4 irony better than humans (P=0.040, r=0.32). Faux pas: GPT-4 below humans (P=5.4e-5, r=0.55), GPT-3.5 near floor (r=0.72), LLaMA2-70B above humans (P=0.002, r=0.44) but illusory. Per-test human N about 48-51. 15 LLM sessions per model.
quote: poor performance of GPT originated from a hyperconservative approach towards committing to conclusions
limits: Text vignettes; only GPT and LLaMA2 families (2023 models). Novel items used as contamination controls.
agent_relevance: GPT-4's low faux pas score came from hyperconservative commitment, not missing inference. Prompting to commit under uncertainty may fix it.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: Failed generalisation of Kosinski's claim that GPT-3.5 has ToM: small logic-preserving changes flip the answer.
numbers: Transparent-bag variant: GPT-3.5 still says Sam believes the bag holds chocolate (P about 95-98%) even when Sam can see inside or cannot read. Cat-in-basket variants: P(box) rises from about 0% to 25-43% in some alterations; the model fails all variations.
limits: One model (GPT-3.5), few hand-made vignettes, no human data; later models (GPT-4) did better in Strachan 2024.
agent_relevance: Pass rates on the original vignette overstate ability. Test own scaffold on perturbed versions.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large LMs are calibrated on multiple choice and can judge their own sampled answers with P(True); a trained P(IK) head predicts whether the model knows the answer.
numbers: Models 800M to 52B. Keeping only answers with P(True)>0.5 improves accuracy on GSM8k, arithmetic, TriviaQA, Lambada, Codex. AUROC values in a 0.6-0.85 range across settings (read from figure labels; not mapped to each setting).
limits: Calibration needs suitable formatting; RLHF policies are miscalibrated unless temperature is tuned; out-of-distribution P(IK) only partial.
agent_relevance: Self-assessment can gate the loop, but verify per task and per model.

source: Wang & Zhao (2023) Metacognitive prompting improves understanding in large language models
finding: A five-step introspective prompt beat chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve on NLU tasks.
numbers: Averaged over Llama2, PaLM2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 zero-shot: BoolQ 89.0 vs CoT 86.3; DDI 73.4 vs 69.4; MedNLI 70.9 vs 67.1; QNLI 92.6 vs 91.2. GPT-4 5-shot MP on BoolQ 98.9 vs CoT-SC 96.8.
limits: Same-lab prompt design, NLU benchmarks only, gains of 1-4 points, no token-matched control.
agent_relevance: Cheap thinking-about-thinking prompts give small gains; test against token-matched controls.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) Demystifying multi-agent debate: the role of confidence and diversity
finding: Vanilla debate often does not beat majority vote. Initial diversity plus calibrated confidence in updates restores gains, importing human deliberation findings.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B: Debate 5x5 below majority vote on GSM8K (0.847 vs 0.908) and CSQA (0.727 vs 0.808). HD+Confidence: GSM8K 0.932, CSQA 0.828, MMLU-FL 0.619 vs 0.548 majority, GPQA 0.361 vs 0.335. Theory: homogeneous debate is a martingale (no expected gain).
limits: Small open models (7-8B), gains of a few points, confidence-modulation training needed.
agent_relevance: Debate among identical agents does nothing in expectation; use diversity and calibrated confidence.

source: From process loss to assembly bonus: human-grounded diagnosis of multi-agent LLM collaboration (2026)
finding: LLM groups show the same assembly-bonus asymmetry as humans (help the average member, not the best) but follow majorities more, share less unique information, and converge earlier.
numbers: Human group chats vs matched LLM traces on Wason-style tasks, then analogical, abductive and analytical tasks. Correct minority signals succeed mainly when re-expressed early. Human-research-inspired interventions gave modest gains (no numbers extracted).
limits: Only abstract and introduction read; per-condition numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: LLM groups conform early. Protect minority answers and force unique-information sharing before convergence.

source: Conformity dynamics in LLM multi-agent systems (2026)
finding: Network topology and a confidence-normalised pooling rule govern conformity in LLM agent groups on misinformation detection.
numbers: Centralised aggregation is fast but sensitive to hub competence and same-model alignment; distributed consensus is more robust (qualitative, from abstract).
limits: Abstract-level only; no effect sizes extracted.
agent_relevance: Avoid a single hub agent from the same model as its workers.

source: Normann, van Emmerik & Morina (2014) first meta-analysis of MCT (cited in Normann & Morina 2018)
finding: First MCT meta-analysis, anxiety and depression only, 5 trials vs CBT.
numbers: MCT vs CBT post-treatment g=0.97 (quoted in the 2018 update).
limits: Not opened; numbers via secondary citation.
agent_relevance: Same as b02.

source: Nordahl et al. (2018) MCT vs CBT trial (cited in Normann & Morina 2018)
finding: Named by the 2018 meta-analysis as the one trial with balanced allegiance (originators of both protocols).
numbers: No numbers extracted.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Most trustworthy comparison; fetch it next if this line matters.

source: Bahrami et al. (2010) Optimally interacting minds (Science), as described in Bahrami 2012
finding: Founding study: dyads sharing confidence beat the better member when sensitivities were similar, matching the weighted confidence sharing model.
numbers: Exact founding-study figures not extracted.
limits: Not opened; secondary description only. Dissimilar dyads did worse than the better member.
agent_relevance: Original source of the similar-sensitivity rule.

source: Mahmoodi et al. (2015) Equality bias impairs collective decision-making across cultures (PNAS)
finding: Reported equality bias (weighting partners equally regardless of ability) in dyads across cultures.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Not opened; from my prior knowledge, verify before use.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: equal weighting fails when abilities differ.

source: Hidden profile paradigm for LLM collective reasoning (arXiv 2505.11556, found by search)
finding: Adapts the human hidden-profile group paradigm to six leading LLMs.
numbers: Not opened; only title and one-line description seen.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Test for whether LLM teams share unique information.

source: Choi et al. (2025) debate as a martingale; Estornell & Liu (2024), as cited in Zhu 2026
finding: Under homogeneous agents and uniform updates, debate preserves expected correctness (no gain). Low diversity makes debate collapse to the initial majority.
numbers: Theory as described in Zhu et al. (2026), eq. 14 and related work.
limits: Not opened directly.
agent_relevance: Debate with identical agents is not a reasoning method.
